summary: Live Science interviews ocean explorer Jon Copley about his new book "Deep Sea: 10 Things You Should Know". He argues the biggest myth is that we know almost nothing about the deep ocean, and says climate-driven deoxygenation is a bigger long-term threat than deep sea mining. He also explains how hydrothermal vents and chemosynthesis widen our view of where life could exist in the cosmos.
one_line: Jon Copley says we know far more about the deep ocean than the moon or Mars, and that climate change-driven deoxygenation is its main threat.
key_facts: Jon Copley is a professor of ocean exploration and science communication at the University of Southampton in the U.K., and has made dozens of deep sea dives over the past 25 years.

His new book "Deep Sea: 10 Things You Should Know" (Orion Publishing, 2023) answers the top 10 questions people have about the deep sea and tackles myths; it follows his 2019 book "Ask an Ocean Explorer" (Hodder & Stoughton), which had 25 chapters.
Copley says the biggest myth is that we know almost nothing about the deep ocean; the claim that we know more about the moon or Mars is only true for a detailed map of the solid surface terrain.
The moon and Mars are not covered in seawater, which blocks radar and forces the use of sonar in the deep ocean, making seafloor mapping harder.
Deep sea mining has not actually started yet, and Copley says research does not support some of the more hyperbolic headlines about it.

Active hydrothermal vents cover just 50 square kilometers (19 square miles) globally and host more than 400 animal species found in no other habitat type, so mining there would risk species extinction.
Copley is confident active hydrothermal vents will receive protection because scientists have been advocating it for years.
Copley considers climate change the biggest human threat to the deep sea, particularly deoxygenation, because deep sea animals get oxygen from seawater.
Warmer water carries less dissolved oxygen and speeds up the metabolism of marine life so oxygen is used faster; melting ice sheets make water fresher and weaken the currents that carry oxygen down.

These deep ocean currents take centuries to complete their journey, so changes already made will be felt for centuries; the deep ocean is on track to have 10% less oxygen globally by 2400 than in preindustrial times.
Recent research has advanced sensory ecology, including how deep sea animals perceive their environment and avoid being seen by predators.
Deep sea vents glow very faintly, too faintly for the human eye but enough for microbes to use as an energy source.
Chemosynthesis, life powered by chemical energy rather than photosynthesis, was thought impossible as a basis for whole animal populations until hydrothermal vents were discovered.
